title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #541** asks about the structure of sequences with uniform zero-sum behavior.

Given p residues modulo a prime p, suppose every nonempty zero-sum subset has the SAME cardinality r. Graham conjectured this forces at most 2 distinct residues in the sequence.

This was proved for large primes by Erdős-Szemerédi (1976) and for all moduli by Gao-Hamidoune-Wang (2010).
mathContext: If $\forall S \subseteq [p],\; S \neq \emptyset,\; \sum_{i \in S} a_i \equiv 0 \pmod{p} \Rightarrow |S| = r$, then $|\{a_1, \ldots, a_p\}| \leq 2$.

title: Imports and Setup
content:
We import Mathlib and enable classical logic. The key types used are:

- **Fin p**: indices 1 to p
- **ZMod p**: integers modulo p as a ring
- **Finset**: finite sets for subset operations
mathContext: Classical logic allows us to work with arbitrary predicates on sets without explicit decidability proofs.

title: HasUniqueZeroSumLength
content:
**HasUniqueZeroSumLength(p, a, r)** captures the key constraint: every nonempty subset S with Σᵢ∈S aᵢ = 0 has exactly |S| = r elements.

This is a very strong uniformity condition. Most sequences have zero-sum subsets of varying sizes; having them all be the same size r is highly restrictive.
mathContext: $\forall S : \text{Finset}(\text{Fin}\; p),\; S \neq \emptyset \to \sum_{i \in S} a_i = 0 \to S.\text{card} = r$

title: HasSomeUniqueZeroSumLength
content:
**HasSomeUniqueZeroSumLength(p, a)** asserts there EXISTS some r with the uniformity property.

This is the hypothesis for Graham's conjecture: we don't specify what r is, just that all zero-sum subsets have the same cardinality.

title: Distinct Count
content:
**distinctCount(p, a)** counts how many distinct residues appear in the sequence.

We use `Set.range a` to get all values taken by a, then `ncard` for the cardinality. This is noncomputable since it involves supremum over potentially infinite sets (though here the range is finite).

title: Graham's Conjecture
content:
**The Main Result**: If all nonempty zero-sum subsets have the same cardinality, then at most 2 distinct residues appear in the sequence.

Intuitively: the uniformity constraint is so strong that it forces the sequence to be 'almost constant'. With 3+ distinct values, one could construct zero-sum subsets of different sizes.

Marked with `sorry` as the full proof is complex.

title: Erdős-Szemerédi (1976)
content:
**For sufficiently large primes p**, Graham's conjecture holds.

Erdős and Szemerédi proved this using combinatorial arguments that work when p exceeds some threshold. The exact threshold depends on the proof technique.
mathContext: $\forall^{\infty} p$ in atTop, $p$ prime $\to (\text{HasSomeUniqueZeroSumLength}(p, a) \to \text{distinctCount}(p, a) \leq 2)$

title: Gao-Hamidoune-Wang (2010)
content:
**The Full Result**: Graham's conjecture holds for ALL moduli n, not just primes!

This 2010 result generalized beyond the prime case, showing the phenomenon is arithmetic rather than purely prime-specific. The proof uses deep techniques from additive combinatorics.

title: Constant Sequence Example
content:
**The trivial case**: if a₁ = a₂ = ... = aₚ = c (all the same), then distinctCount ≤ 1.

For constant sequences, Σᵢ∈S aᵢ = |S|·c ≡ 0 iff |S| ≡ 0 mod ord(c). All zero-sum subsets have cardinality divisible by the order of c.

title: Two-Value Example
content:
**Two distinct values also work**: alternating between c and d gives distinctCount ≤ 2.

The proof shows the range is contained in {c, d}, then uses Set.ncard properties to bound the cardinality.

Note: this doesn't prove the sequence HAS the unique zero-sum length property, just that if it did, distinctCount ≤ 2 would hold.
mathContext: $\text{range}(\lambda i \mapsto \text{if } i\%2=0 \text{ then } c \text{ else } d) \subseteq \{c,d\} \to \text{ncard} \leq 2$

title: Why 3+ Values Fail
content:
**The Key Insight**: With 3 or more distinct values {a, b, c}, one can construct zero-sum subsets of DIFFERENT cardinalities.

The argument involves:
1. Using copies of a alone (if a·k ≡ 0)
2. Mixing a's and b's in different proportions
3. Introducing c's to create new combinations

These lead to zero-sums of varying sizes, contradicting the uniformity hypothesis.
mathContext: 3+ distinct values $\Rightarrow \exists S, T$ with $\sum_{i \in S} a_i = \sum_{i \in T} a_i = 0$ but $|S| \neq |T|$

title: Zero-Sum Existence (Olson)
content:
**Zero-sum subsequences always exist** in Z/pZ by the pigeonhole principle.

Consider partial sums s₀=0, s₁=a₁, s₂=a₁+a₂, ..., sₚ=Σaᵢ. These p+1 values in Z/pZ (which has p elements) must have a collision: sᵢ = sⱼ for some i < j. Then Σₖ∈{i+1,...,j} aₖ = sⱼ - sᵢ = 0.

Marked `sorry` as the detailed proof is nontrivial.

title: Historical Context
content:
**Zero-Sum Theory**: This problem belongs to additive combinatorics, studying when subsets of abelian groups must contain zero-sum subsequences.

**Key Results**:
- **Davenport constant**: minimum length ensuring zero-sum exists
- **Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv (1961)**: 2n-1 integers contain n with sum ≡ 0 (mod n)
- **Olson's work**: bounds on zero-sum subsequence lengths

Graham's question captures an extremal phenomenon: strong uniformity forces simplicity.
mathContext: Zero-sum theory: when must subsets of $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^k$ contain zero-sum subsequences?

title: Erdős-Ginzburg-Ziv Theorem
content:
**The EGZ Theorem (1961)**: Among any 2n-1 integers, some n of them have sum divisible by n.

This is a foundational result in zero-sum theory. It's tight: 2n-2 integers may avoid having n sum to 0 mod n (e.g., n-1 copies of 0 and n-1 copies of 1).

Stated as an axiom since the proof is nontrivial.
